To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
mucosal immunization with HIV envelope proteins can induce HIV-specific IgA, T helper and cytotoxic T lymphocyte responses, and that these responses are adjuvanted by TLR agonists.

mucosal vaccine administration of HIV envelope protein immunogen and adjuvant is more effective at inducing immune responses than parenteral administration; mucosal vaccine administration is also more effective than parenterally administered vaccines at protecting nonhuman primates from mucosal challenge with simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV); and, mucosal administration of SIV envelope protein immunogen with adjuvant induces mucosal and systemic antibody responses, and mucosal CD4+ T cell responses, that correlate with protection

mucosal immunization with recombinant HIV envelope protein and/or DNA vaccine vectors encoding the envelope protein can elicit mucosal and systemic immune responses, and that Toll-like receptor agonist adjuvants may enhance the magnitude of mucosal and systemic antibody and cellular responses.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing mucosal vaccines that can induce protective immunity against HIV in mucosal tissues, and with understanding mechanisms of mucosal immune responses to HIV.
the development of effective mucosal vaccines for the prevention of HIV transmission.
the design of mucosal vaccine approaches that will elicit protective mucosal and systemic immunity to HIV and SIV in animal models.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
mucosal vaccine strategies for HIV are still at an early stage and that the field is wide open for novel ideas.
the field has yet to achieve a mucosal vaccine that can prevent or reduce HIV transmission.

mucosal immunization with HIV envelope protein immunogen plus adjuvant has been shown to induce mucosal and systemic antibody responses, but these responses are insufficient to protect against HIV infection in nonhuman primate challenge studies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
mucosal immunization with HIV envelope protein immunogen, with or without adjuvant, can induce both humoral and cellular mucosal immune responses.

mucosal immunization with HIV protein antigens is feasible in humans and nonhuman primate models, but that the magnitude of immune responses is often lower than that achieved by parenteral immunization.

mucosal vaccines can induce protective immunity in the gut mucosa and genital tract, but the magnitude of the immune response is highly dependent on the route of immunization, the vaccine formulation and the adjuvant.
The main takeaway from our work is that

mucosal immunization with HIV protein immunogens, including gp120, gp140 and gp160, is effective in generating HIV-specific mucosal and systemic antibody responses, and can also elicit mucosal and systemic HIV-specific T cell responses.

mucosal vaccines are a promising approach to HIV prevention, but the development of mucosal vaccines will be a slow process requiring careful preclinical evaluation and extensive testing of candidate vaccines in humans.
mucosal vaccine strategies can be used to elicit immune responses at mucosal surfaces and to induce immune responses that may be protective against HIV infection.
